title: Occipital seizures and persistent homonymous hemianopia with T2 hypointensity on MRI in nonketotic hyperglycemia
case_prompt:
A 53-year-old Indian man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease presented with sudden visual impairment in both eyes followed minutes later by a brief generalized tonic–clonic seizure. He had no prior history of epilepsy or substance abuse, but a history of skin abscesses attributed to poor glycemic control. In the emergency department, he was postictal—agitated and drowsy—without focal deficits. Laboratory studies showed:  
• Random plasma glucose, 581 mg/dL; HbA1c, 11.4%; serum ketones, negative.  
• Serum sodium, 136 mEq/L; creatinine, 2.9 mg/dL.  
Lumbar puncture yielded normal cerebrospinal fluid, and noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. Intravenous phenytoin, insulin infusion, and hydration were initiated. 

After regaining consciousness, examination revealed a complete right homonymous hemianopia. Multiple brief complex partial seizures were observed, characterized by rightward head and eye deviation, right-sided nystagmus, and impaired awareness, each lasting about 60 seconds. Brain MRI demonstrated focal hypointensity in the left occipital lobe on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences. Conventional scalp EEG recorded three seizures, each beginning with high-amplitude fast activity over the left occipital region with ipsilateral and contralateral spread, followed by gradual postictal slowing.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Migraine was considered given the visual symptoms — “Possible differential diagnosis includes migraine, stroke/transient ischemic attack, or posterior reversible encephalopathy.”  
2. Stroke or transient ischemic attack was considered due to acute homonymous hemianopia — “Possible differential diagnosis includes migraine, stroke/transient ischemic attack, or posterior reversible encephalopathy.”  
3. Posterior reversible encephalopathy was considered because seizures and visual disturbances can occur in PRES — “Possible differential diagnosis includes migraine, stroke/transient ischemic attack, or posterior reversible encephalopathy.”  
4. Postictal Todd’s phenomenon was considered to explain the prolonged hemianopia after seizure — “This prolonged visual deficit has previously been reported in hyperglycemia, possibly a postictal Todd's phenomena or epilepsia partialis continua.”  
5. Epilepsia partialis continua was considered for ongoing focal seizure activity manifesting as persistent visual field loss — “This prolonged visual deficit has previously been reported in hyperglycemia, possibly a postictal Todd's phenomena or epilepsia partialis continua.”  
6. Occipital seizures in the setting of nonketotic hyperglycemia were considered most consistent with the clinical, EEG, MRI, and laboratory findings — “Occipital seizures in hyperglycemic states have been described with blood glucose levels ranging from 200 mg/dl to over 500 mg/dl.”
